articles.title: Assédio em Varginha: servidores denunciam superintendente regional | G1
articles.standfirst: Servidores da Secretaria de Estado de Educação relatam episódios de humilhação, perseguição e assédio atribuídos à superintendente regional de ensino.
articles.summary: Servidores da Educação em Varginha relatam episódios de perseguição e humilhação pela superintendente regional, resultando em condenação judicial do Estado de Minas Gerais.
articles.body:
Servidores da Secretaria de Estado de Educação de Minas Gerais denunciaram condutas atribuídas à superintendente regional de ensino de Varginha , Eliane dos Reis Dias. Os relatos incluem acusações de assédio, humilhação, perseguição e ameaças no ambiente de trabalho. Um dos casos resultou em uma decisão judicial que condenou o Estado de Minas Gerais ao pagamento de R$ 4 mil por danos morais a um servidor.

Um servidor, que pediu para não ser identificado, afirmou que sofreu um episódio de assédio em 2021, no primeiro dia de trabalho. Segundo ele, a situação ocorreu no gabinete da superintendente regional de ensino.

"Ela me chamou na sala e falou que tinha um presente ali, geralmente é um presente que ela dava para quem era novato. E ao abrir a caixa, era um pênis de borracha e tinha duas pessoas ali que presenciaram a situação. Eu fiquei impactado, tive um constrangimento e quem estava ali perto levou em tons de brincadeira", relatou o servidor.

Servidores denunciam assédio e perseguição por superintendente regional de ensino de Varginha — Foto: Reprodução EPTV

De acordo com ele, anos depois, em 2024, passou a sofrer perseguição após questionamentos sobre possíveis irregularidades na contratação de inspetores.

O servidor afirma que a situação foi denunciada à Ouvidoria do Estado. Sem avanços, segundo ele, um grupo de servidores enviou um e-mail a um deputado estadual pedindo ajuda. Ainda de acordo com o relato, o conteúdo da denúncia foi posteriormente exposto pela superintendente durante uma reunião.

"Ela expôs no telão o teor da denúncia, da manifestação e do pedido de ajuda ao deputado. E ali tinham os nomes de quem pediu ajuda, no qual ela colocava isso em dúvida, colocava o profissionalismo desses servidores em dúvida, no qual causou toda a repercussão. Na sala tinha aproximadamente 40 pessoas, segundo ainda a lista de presença que foi colhida ali", afirmou.

Outra servidora, que também preferiu não se identificar, relatou que está em tratamento psicológico após problemas envolvendo a superintendente. Segundo ela, houve ameaças e outros colegas também teriam adoecido em razão do ambiente de trabalho.

"A pessoa acaba se adoecendo mesmo, porque não é só o meu caso que estou doente até hoje. Tem muitos outros colegas que estão sem condições de trabalhar, sabe? Porque se adoeceram e muitos têm medo de procurar a justiça, porque tem medo de retaliação por parte dela", disse.

As denúncias de assédio foram levadas ao Ministério Público. Após ouvir alguns servidores e a própria superintendente, a 7ª Promotoria arquivou o caso. Conforme o documento citado na reportagem, os fatos narrados foram considerados relevantes para eventual apuração disciplinar, mas não para atribuição de responsabilidade pelo Ministério Público.

O mesmo documento ressalta que os casos poderiam ser levados à Justiça. Um dos servidores optou por ingressar com ação judicial. Em decisão assinada pela juíza Luana Vilma de Souza, o Estado de Minas Gerais foi condenado a pagar R$ 4 mil ao servidor por danos morais. A decisão ainda cabe recurso.

O advogado da vítima, Cristiano de Oliveira Corrêa, destacou a importância da denúncia de casos de assédio.

"Assédio é crime, ainda mais quando se trata de uma servidora pública, que o máximo que a gente espera é uma conduta ética profissional, por ser uma servidora concursada do Estado", afirmou.

Procurada, a superintendente citada na reportagem informou que a assessoria de comunicação da Educação encaminharia uma resposta. Já a Secretaria de Estado de Educação, por meio da Advocacia-Geral do Estado, declarou apenas que não comenta processos judiciais.

articles.title: Houthis anunciam ataques contra Arábia Saudita | G1
articles.standfirst: Também nesta segunda (5), a Turquia e o Paquistão anunciaram que farão uma "mobilização rápida" de tropas na Arábia Saudita como parte de uma nova aliança de defesa.
articles.summary: Também nesta segunda (5), a Turquia e o Paquistão anunciaram que farão uma "mobilização rápida" de tropas na Arábia Saudita como parte de uma nova aliança de defesa.
articles.body:
Imagens de drones mostram ataques contra veículos e tropas na rodovia costeira sul, perto de Al Bahiya, província de Lahij, no Iêmen — Foto: Mídia militar Houthis / Divulgação

Os Houthis, grupo extremista do Iêmen apoiado pelo Irã , anunciaram uma série de ataques contra a Arábia Saudita nesta segunda-feira (5).

O porta-voz dos rebeldes ienamitas afirmou que o aeroporto internacional da capital saudita, Riad, uma refinaria da Aramco e locais em todo o sul do reino saudita foram atingidos.

Os ataques, que incluíram drones, mísseis balísticos e de cruzeiro, "tiveram como alvo o Aeroporto Internacional Rei Khalid em Riade", disse Yahya Saree, acrescentando que "a refinaria da Aramco em Rabigh" também foi atingida, juntamente com instalações militares e aeroportos menores no sul.

Os bombardeios foram uma resposta a uma ofensiva lançada pelo governo do Iêmen horas antes.

Os militares iemenitas disseram que realizaram mais de 1.000 ataques, com o apoio de 100 aviões de guerra, fornecidos pela coalizão liderada pela Arábia Saudita - que apoia o governo -, contra a capital do país, Saná, que há anos está nas mãos dos Houthis, desde o amanhecer.

O porta-voz da coalizão informou na rede social X que suas forças navais tinham "destruídos depósitos de armas, instalações onde foram armazenadas embarcações com armadilhas explosivas e minas navais e que tinham "frustrado um plano de ataque" contra vias navegáveis ​​no sul do Mar Vermelho.

Também nesta segunda, a Turquia e o Paquistão anunciaram que farão uma "mobilização rápida" de tropas na Arábia Saudita como parte de uma nova aliança de defesa, sem especificar que função os militares mobilizados desempenhariam.

No dia 25 de setembro, foi a vez da França fazer o mesmo (veja no vídeo abaixo) .

A ofensiva do governo do Iêmen nesta segunda havia sido anunciada um dia antes. O chefe do Conselho Presidencial, Rashad al Alimi, disse que o objetivo dela, que recebeu o nome de "Amanhecer do Iêmen ", é recuperar a totalidade do território.

O porta-voz da coalizão militar liderada pela Arábia Saudita diz que dará "apoio aéreo 24 horas por dia às forças armadas iemenitas" e irá garantir "a proteção aérea do Estreito de Bab el Mandeb", rota estratégica para o comércio marítimo internacional.

Após a troca de ataques, o secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres, expressou sua preocupação com a "forte escalada" dos combates no Iêmen e condenou os ataques dos houthis em território saudita.

Em setembro, os Houthis impuseram um bloqueio militar contra o governo saudita no Mar Vermelho e reforçaram o seu controle sobre esse estreito, cuja importância aumentou depois que o Irã impôs fortes restrições à navegação no Ormuz, do outro lado da península arábica, no âmbito da guerra no Oriente Médio.

articles.title: Trump diz achar que Irã é responsável por ataque em voo da FlyDubai | G1
articles.standfirst: O presidente americano também afirmou que uma ameaça levou os Estados Unidos a retirar bombardeiros de uma base aérea no Reino Unido.
articles.summary: O presidente americano também afirmou que uma ameaça levou os Estados Unidos a retirar bombardeiros de uma base aérea no Reino Unido.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , afirmou nesta segunda-feira (5) que acredita que o Irã foi o responsável pelo ataque em um voo da FlyDubai para Israel , na semana passada.

Ao ser questionado por jornalistas sobre o incidente e sua motivação, que segue sendo investigada, Trump afirmou:

O presidente americano também confirmou relatos de que os EUA retiraram bombardeiros de uma base aérea no Reino Unido e falou que uma ameaça levou à decisão.

"Havia algumas ameaças, e em vez de provocar o inimigo — vamos capturar o inimigo e derrotá-lo, mas por que deveríamos deixá-los lá? —, nós os transferimos um pouco, não muito longe", disse.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, conversa com a imprensa antes de embarcar no helicóptero Marine One rumo a Grand Island, Nebraska — Foto: REUTERS/Eric Lee

Os Emirados Árabes Unidos disseram neste sábado (3) que o copiloto do voo da FlyDubai atacou o comandante com um machado de emergência e tentou assumir o controle da aeronave durante o incidente ocorrido na quarta-feira (30).

Até então, não estava claro qual arma havia sido usada no ataque. Segundo o procurador-geral dos Emirados, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, o episódio foi uma tentativa de ato "terrorista"

O voo FZ1073, que seguia de Dubai para Tel Aviv, transportava mais de 170 passageiros e tripulantes quando o incidente aconteceu na quarta-feira.

Passageiros e tripulantes conseguiram dominar o copiloto. Um piloto reserva da FlyDubai que estava a bordo assumiu o controle da aeronave e pousou no aeroporto de Tabuk, no noroeste da Arábia Saudita, onde o copiloto foi detido.

Segundo a Reuters, o copiloto foi identificado como Hammam al-Hammami, cidadão de Omã, por uma fonte com conhecimento direto do caso. As autoridades dos Emirados Árabes Unidos não confirmaram imediatamente a identidade.

A investigação ainda está em andamento para determinar as circunstâncias do episódio, a motivação do copiloto e se houve outras pessoas envolvidas. As autoridades também analisam evidências físicas e digitais.

A classificação do episódio como tentativa de ataque "terrorista" é a primeira feita publicamente por uma autoridade dos Emirados. Até então, as circunstâncias e a motivação do ataque ainda eram investigadas.

A FlyDubai afirmou que as circunstâncias do incidente continuam sob investigação e que a companhia não está em posição de comentar mais detalhes.

O avião saiu de Dubai com destino a Tel Aviv. Durante o voo sobre a Arábia Saudita, a aeronave perdeu cerca de 5 mil metros de altitude em pouco mais de 30 segundos, segundo dados do Flightradar24.

O comandante foi atacado dentro da cabine. A nova versão apresentada pelas autoridades dos Emirados afirma que o copiloto usou um machado de emergência, equipamento mantido na cabine para situações de emergência.

Depois do ataque, o comandante conseguiu abrir a porta da cabine. Passageiros e tripulantes ajudaram a conter o copiloto, enquanto outro piloto que estava a bordo assumiu os controles.

A aeronave pousou em segurança em Tabuk, na Arábia Saudita.

Autoridades dos Emirados e de Israel participam da investigação. Os investigadores buscam esclarecer o que aconteceu dentro da cabine, a motivação do copiloto e se ele agiu sozinho ou recebeu orientação de outras pessoas.

O primeiro-ministro de Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, havia dito anteriormente que o copiloto era cidadão de Omã e que poderia ter passado por radicalização islamista. Ele também afirmou que ainda não havia sido estabelecida uma motivação definitiva para o ataque. A investigação continua.

O avião que transportava passageiros que estavam no voo da FlyDubai com destino a Israel, saído dos Emirados Árabes Unidos e desviado para a Arábia Saudita após emitir um sinal de emergência, chega ao Aeroporto Internacional Ben Gurion, em Lod, perto de Tel Aviv, Israel. — Foto: Ammar Awad / Reuters

articles.title: He arrived in Canada as a refugee more than 50 years ago; now an anonymous donor has created scholarships across every province and territory
articles.summary: The story of an anonymous Canadian donor began with a move made more than five decades ago, when he arrived in Canada as a refugee with no money.
articles.body: The story of an anonymous Canadian donor began with a move made more than five decades ago, when he arrived in Canada as a refugee with no money. An unexpected university grant helped him complete his education and changed the course of his life. Decades later, after building a successful career and contributing to Canada’s technology and innovation economy, he began giving back. His philanthropy has now reached universities across every Canadian province and territory, with scholarships designed to help students continue their education and build their own futures.A refugee’s journey led to scholarships across CanadaThe donor arrived in Canada in 1968, according to the University of Regina, which profiled his story in its September 2026 Donor Impact Report. He came without money, but his circumstances changed when the university he attended provided unexpected financial support.That assistance allowed him to graduate. The experience stayed with him long after he completed his studies. He later recalled that, even at the time, he already knew he would want to help other students facing financial difficulties if he ever had the opportunity.More than 50 years after arriving in Canada, that early experience has become the foundation of a wide-ranging approach to philanthropy. The University of Regina reports that he has created scholarships in every province and territory to mark his 50th anniversary in Canada, while choosing to remain anonymous.How one unexpected opportunity shaped his lifeInstead of treating the support he received as something that ended with his graduation, he carried the experience into his later life.After earning his degree, he went on to have substantial success in his career and made significant contributions to Canada’s innovation economy and technology development, the University of Regina says. His later decision to become a philanthropist connected his professional life with an earlier personal experience of receiving help when he needed it.The scholarships became one way of extending that opportunity to students who might otherwise struggle to continue their education.What the VK to C in 50 scholarship supportsThe ‘VK to C in 50 scholarship’ was established in 2018. It initially recognised students who demonstrated academic achievement and leadership, while also showing a commitment to tolerance, respect and responsible citizenship.The award also looks at how students contribute to university life and the wider community. The University of Regina says the scholarship was later designated specifically for students enrolled in science, technology, engineering or mathematics programmes, reflecting the donor’s own background and his contributions to Canadian innovation.The change gives the scholarship a closer connection to the donor’s academic experience. He studied physics and has explained that he feels particularly connected to students pursuing similar scientific fields.The University of Regina has already seen the scholarship’s impactAt the University of Regina, the VK to C in 50 scholarship has supported 3 students since 2019, according to the university. Those recipients have pursued degrees in different areas, including Systems Engineering, Psychology, and Kinesiology and Health Studies.The range of subjects represented among the recipients shows how the scholarship has supported individual students on different academic paths. Its more recent STEM designation reflects the donor’s decision to place greater emphasis on science and related fields.Why the donor chose to remain anonymousThe decision to keep his identity private is central to the way the scholarship was created. The donor told the University of Regina that the student receiving the award should remain the focus, while his own name is not important to that purpose.That approach also explains why details about his philanthropy have emerged through the university without identifying him. The scholarship carries the name VK to C in 50, but the person behind it has continued to give anonymously.His reasoning is straightforward. The award is intended to help students continue their studies, rather than make the donor the centre of attention.A personal experience became a long-term commitmentThe donor’s approach to giving is rooted in gratitude for the country and the educational opportunity he received after arriving as a refugee. The University of Regina says his guiding principle is to give in return for the opportunities Canada provided and to help others gain the chance to succeed.That principle has extended far beyond a single university. By creating scholarships in every province and territory to mark his 50 years in Canada, he has turned one act of financial support into a continuing commitment to students across the country. For the recipients, the scholarships are practical support at a point when financial assistance can make continuing a degree possible.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Russia’s defence budget jumps 27% to $202 billion: Putin takes military spending to Cold War-era levels
articles.summary: Russia is preparing to spend a staggering 17.1 trillion roubles, or about $202.6 billion, on defence in 2027, up 27 percent from the 13.5 trillion roubles
articles.body: Russia is preparing to spend a staggering 17.1 trillion roubles, or about $202.6 billion, on defence in 2027, up 27 percent from the 13.5 trillion roubles earlier allocated for the year and one of the largest military budgets since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991.The proposed spending, disclosed in Russian government budget documents reviewed by Reuters, underlines how deeply the Ukraine war has reshaped Moscow's economic priorities, with defence set to absorb about 6.9 percent of Russia's projected economic output.The scale of the increase becomes clearer when viewed against Russia's pre-war spending. Defence expenditure has surged since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, rising from roughly 3 percent of GDP in the early war years to nearly 7 percent under the proposed 2027 allocation.Russia's military burden has now reached levels that invite comparisons with the Soviet era.Since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia has not allocated such a large share of its economy to defence. The proposed 6.9 percent of GDP is comparable with the heavy military burden seen during some of the Soviet Union's most intense Cold War years.In 1989, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev disclosed that the Soviet Union's defence spending stood at 77.3 billion roubles, equivalent to about $124 billion at the official exchange rate at the time. The figure represented roughly 8.4 percent of the Soviet Union's GDP, according to contemporary assessments.At that time, western governments and analysts disputed the figure. The UK government estimated that Soviet military outlays, calculated using Nato-style definitions, were roughly twice the officially disclosed amount and accounted for around 15 to 17 percent of Soviet GDP.The 2027 allocation also comes despite growing pressure on Russia's finances. Moscow is facing lower projected oil and gas revenues, a wider budget deficit and increased borrowing, yet the Kremlin is continuing to prioritise military expenditure. The result is a Russian economy increasingly geared towards sustaining a prolonged war effort rather than returning to pre-war spending patterns.Russia's defence spending has surged since the Ukraine invasion, rising from around 3 to 4 trillion roubles before the war to 4.7 trillion in 2022, 6.4 trillion in 2023 and about 10.8 trillion in 2024. Spending climbed further in 2025, while the proposed 17.1 trillion roubles for 2027 would mark a dramatic increase from pre-war levels.As the Ukraine war intensifies, the surge in defence spending is expected to help Moscow sustain its military campaign and replenish weapons and equipment lost on the battlefield.The additional funding will support Russia's defence-industrial base, including production of missiles, drones, artillery ammunition, armoured vehicles and other military equipment, while also covering troop salaries, recruitment incentives and the replacement of battlefield losses.

articles.title: Two young Minnesota farmers started grazing sheep under solar panels in 2017; their flock has now grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms
articles.summary: In 2017, Arlo Hark and Josie Trople founded Cannon Valley Graziers in Northfield, Minnesota, as a dedicated solar grazing operation.
articles.body: In 2017, Arlo Hark and Josie Trople founded Cannon Valley Graziers in Northfield, Minnesota, as a dedicated solar grazing operation. According to the North American Agrivoltaics Awards, the business has now grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms for developers, operators and owners. Its flock rotates across dozens of sites each season in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Iowa, with further sites in the western and central United States. The company offers Solar Grazing, Vegetation Management and Forestry Restoration, and has two sister ventures, Tethera and Bayl. The pair have been named the 2026 Solar Ranchers of the Year.How Minnesota farmers started solar grazingArlo and Josie founded Cannon Valley Graziers in Northfield, Minnesota, in 2017. It describes the business as a dedicated solar grazing operation that has now grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms for developers, operators and owners.The business started in the upper Midwest. Cannon Valley Graziers now rotates its flock across dozens of sites each season in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Iowa, and also grazes solar farms further afield in the western and central United States.How grazing-based vegetation management worksThe company's work now spans three service lines: Solar Grazing, Vegetation Management and Forestry Restoration. It describes Arlo and Josie as experts with applied experience in the field, who have combined these services into a single offering of grazing-based vegetation management.This approach costs less than mowing. It also builds soil health and biodiversity rather than simply suppressing growth, and it keeps working land working with natural systems. The citation says this operating model has earned Cannon Valley Graziers coverage from Bloomberg, Minnesota Public Radio and other media.How the couple expanded the businessArlo holds a board seat at the American Solar Grazing Association. It says he shares leadership responsibilities with other board members and passes on the field-tested lessons that he and Josie have learned over the nearly ten years of building the business, which the citation says now has a footprint across the country.The couple have launched two sister ventures: Tethera, which focuses on meat, and Bayl, which focuses on renewable fibre. Both turn the flock's vegetation-management work into finished products, so that the business draws on food, renewable fibre and fashion, and grazing. Arlo and Josie, as younger farmers with a young family, say their experience shows that solar grazing can give the next generation of agricultural producers access to working land. articles.title: AWS CEO Matt Garman says data centers aren’t using as much water as claimed; debunks 4 ‘popular myths’; says ‘There are clearly …’
articles.summary: AWS CEO Matt Garman recently pushed back against growing criticism of data centers, calling four common claims about their impact “myths.” In a long blog
articles.body: AWS CEO Matt Garman recently pushed back against growing criticism of data centers, calling four common claims about their impact “myths.” In a long blog post, Matt Garman addressed concerns over water consumption, rising electricity rates, pollution from backup diesel generators and the benefits data centers bring to local communities. He argued that data centers use far less water than often claimed, are not solely responsible for higher power bills and rarely run their backup generators. Garman also said data centers generate billions of dollars in tax revenue, create jobs and support schools, emergency services and other local projects in communities where they operate.“There are clearly areas in which the technology and energy industries can be doing better (along with their government partners) but just like in the past when the country has banded together to accomplish something that’s critical for our national security and economic prosperity—we should approach this as a long-term mission that the private and public sectors pursue together,” Garman said adding “Let’s start with some of the myths floating around”.Here are data center myths debunked by AWS CEO Matt GarmanMyth #1: Data centers are taking all of our waterThis is false. Data centers actually use very little water relative to other industries. Direct data center water consumption is about 0.5% of total U.S. direct industrial water use—orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries. For instance, U.S. golf courses alone use ~200x more water than all of Amazon’s data centers—more in about two days than we use in a full year. And, in a recent study of major U.S. industries that collectively account for ~50% of U.S. industrial GDP, data centers ranked lowest in water withdrawals while delivering the highest economic value per gallon.One of the most common soundbites repeated about water is that a typical data center uses five million gallons per day. This is also false. The reality is that a typical data center uses, on average, about 170,000 gallons per day. And at Amazon, our average data center uses less than 13,000 gallons per day (the equivalent of just 42 U.S. households).Myth #2: Data center providers are responsible for driving up all the energy ratesThis is misleading and convenient scapegoating. First, the facts: if you look across states with large numbers of data centers, costs have gone up in some (e.g., Illinois, New York), down in some (e.g., Indiana and Mississippi), and grown slower than the national average in places like Texas. In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived. About 70% of the power lines were built over 25 years ago, with many dating back to the 1960s and 1970s. The capacity and performance needed hasn’t scaled with the rapid growth of digital and AI demand, and the accelerated adoption of AI is precipitating a build-out that was destined to happen—it’s just happening faster than most folks imagined. And, once we collectively build out this new capacity, again funded by the private sector, it should lead to flat or lower rates in the future for residents living in communities with these expanded grids, which we’re already seeing in some states such as Mississippi, Georgia, and Indiana. For our data centers, we work directly with utilities to understand the funds that are necessary to support our projects (e.g., new transmission lines, substations, and other grid upgrades) and then ensure that the revenue we provide to the utility is sufficient to pay for these requirements.Myth #3: Data centers emit huge amounts of pollution with their large backup diesel generatorsThis is also untrue. Most of the services consumers, businesses, and governments rely on every day (e.g., 911 calls, stock markets, healthcare and banking apps, ride-hailing apps like Uber and Lyft, ChatGPT) depend on data centers functioning. As a result, data centers have backup power available in case of a power outage. Some do this through diesel generators that sit idle most of the year. However, when those generators are installed, companies need to get permits for the full potential emissions—what those generators would produce if they ran for the maximum hours under the permit. Critics then see those permits and say things like “…the generators could emit up to 249.9 tons per year each of nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds.” The truth is data center generators almost never run. They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing). And even when backup generators do run, much of the industry now uses Tier 4 emission controls (the cleanest EPA emission standard), so annual NOx emissions from an average data center are the same as a single round trip flight from Seattle to London.Myth #4: Community members get nothing from data centersThis is also false. Data centers bring considerable tax revenue, positive economic impact, large numbers of good jobs, education programs and other benefits to the communities where they’re built. Data center operators are often the single largest taxpayer in a community, with upfront payments routinely exceeding entire annual municipal budgets in the first year of construction, and long-term tax revenue often exceeding prior land use revenue by more than 1,000%. For example, in St. Joseph County, Indiana, the taxes Amazon will pay to the county are estimated to exceed $3 billion, while the prior use on the same land would have paid just $1.2 million over the same term. In Montgomery County, Missouri, our project will pay more than $1.8 billion in taxes over 25 years, while the prior use would have generated about $200,000 (0.01% of what we’ll pay in taxes) over the same period. A 2026 report by Mangum Economics for the Northern Virginia Technology Council estimates that without data center revenue, the average homeowner in Loudoun County, Virginia would pay additional property taxes of $5,800 per year.This new revenue from data centers often not only dramatically reduces the taxes paid by families, but it also funds investments in schools, fire and police departments, parks, roads, and other community services. This is on top of the direct investments most data center companies make to local organizations that are used to address issues most important to them, such as modernized emergency dispatch services, clean energy projects, and support for local food banks. Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.Additionally, thousands of construction jobs are created to build data centers. These jobs benefit families in these communities and are a boon for local small businesses. The average wages paid far exceed local and national medians, and the job numbers associated with these projects are typically very significant compared to the size of these communities. For example, in Madison County, Mississippi (population: 116,000), where we have two data center sites under construction, there are over 2,300 people currently employed in construction; and in Newton County, Georgia (population: 125,000), there are over 1,500 people currently employed. Many jobs are also created to operate a data center once it’s complete. For example, for the data centers in Madison County, we will employ over 1,700 people, and in Newton County, we will employ 400 people. And, we have over 20 education and workforce development programs to help ensure these jobs are available to people from the community, and over 10,000 learners and educators are participating in our programs across 15 data center regions. You can read more about those and our other education programs here.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Azerbaijani woman spent decades collecting miniature books; her museum now holds about 8,000 from 76 countries
articles.summary: An Azerbaijani woman’s decades-long interest in miniature books has grown into a museum containing about 8,000 tiny publications from 76 countries.
articles.body: An Azerbaijani woman’s decades-long interest in miniature books has grown into a museum containing about 8,000 tiny publications from 76 countries. The Museum of Miniature Books stands in Baku’s Old City, close to the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, where books small enough to resemble postage stamps or matchboxes are displayed behind glass. Founded by Zarifa Salakhova, the museum brings together religious texts, literary classics, rare editions and unusually small works from different parts of the world. What began as a personal collection has become a permanent public display devoted entirely to the unique art of miniature publishing.How did Zarifa Salakhova build the miniature book museumThe collection began long before the museum opened. According to AzerbaijanTravel, Salakhova acquired an 1835 facsimile edition of Ivan Krylov’s Fables in Moscow in 1982. That purchase developed into a serious interest in miniature books, eventually leading her to gather editions from different countries over many years. AZERTAC (The Azerbaijan State News Agency) reports that she spent more than 30 years building the private collection before opening it to visitors in 2002.What can visitors find inside the Baku collectionThe museum opened in 2002 in Icherisheher, the historic Old City of Baku. It is situated near the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, according to the Soyqirim Memorial Complex.Today, AzerbaijanTravel reports that around 8,000 miniature publications from 76 countries are held there. The books cover many subjects and genres, with some no larger than a matchbox or postage stamp. It notes that the largest books in the collection do not exceed 10 by 10 centimetres in size.The museum’s displays also show how varied miniature publishing can be. AZERTAC reports that visitors can find religious books, prayer books, works about art, fairy tales and books about cities and countries. Literary works by authors including Alexander Pushkin, Fyodor Dostoyevsky and Nikolai Gogol are also represented.Which rare books give the collection its characterSome of the museum’s most striking items are old and exceptionally small editions. AZERTAC describes a 17th-century miniature Quran as the oldest book in the collection. Another notable item is A History of England, published in London in 1815. AZERTAC also records an edition of Yevgeniy Onegin published in St Petersburg in 1837.The size of some books is even more remarkable than their age. AzerbaijanTravel says the collection includes a book measuring just 2 by 2 millimetres, with a magnifying glass needed to see its text and illustrations. AZERTAC reports several micro-books between 2 and 10 millimetres and identifies Japanese and German examples among the rarest pieces.World Literature Today provides an even closer look at the tiny scale of the collection. Writer J. R. Patterson describes a Japanese edition of Flowers of the Four Seasons measuring three-quarters of a millimetre square, with 22 illustrated pages and its own magnifying glass.How does the museum bring together books from different placesThe collection is international not only in where its books were published but also in the languages and traditions they represent. AZERTAC says the museum contains books in Azerbaijani, Russian, English and German, alongside works from numerous countries.Azerbaijan.az(official state portal of the Republic of Azerbaijan) lists miniature books from Azerbaijan, Russia, the United States, Japan, England, France, Italy, Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Cuba, Switzerland and the former Soviet Union. The Soyqirim Memorial Complex also notes that books signed by well-known figures from former Soviet countries and other nations have entered the collection, along with 40 unique miniatures by American artists.World Literature Today describes displays arranged largely by country of publication. Its account includes familiar titles such as The Call of the Wild, Alice in Wonderland and The Lord of the Rings, as well as a 40-volume edition of Shakespeare’s complete works published in 1841.Why did the collection become a world record holderThe museum’s scale eventually brought international recognition. AZERTAC reported in March 2022 that the Baku Museum of Miniature Books had held the Guinness World Records title for the world’s largest collection of miniature books since 2014.The collection has also continued to attract visitors. The Soyqirim Memorial Complex describes the museum as a popular destination for both local and foreign tourists. Salakhova’s long collecting effort brought together religious works, literature, history and art in a format where even a familiar book can become something entirely different.You use AI every day. articles.title: SC seeks EC response on changes during SIR: Why has Form 6 become a flashpoint — explained
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday raised questions over changes made to Form 6, the application used for registering a voter, during the Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday raised questions over changes made to Form 6, the application used for registering a voter, during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The issue came up while the court was hearing petitions alleging that several decisions linked to the SIR exercise were taken without the approval of all three election commissioners, particularly Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, who were at odds with poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar on multiple occasions.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from the Election Commission, the Centre, the CEC and the other two election commissioners before examining whether the poll panel's statutory procedure was followed.The bench, however, refused to pass an immediate order seeking the suspension of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, while considering the controversy over Form 6, which was one of the central issues raised in the petitions.What is Form 6Form 6 is the application through which an eligible person seeks inclusion of their name in the electoral roll. The Election Commission's guidelines states the application is addressed to the Electoral Registration Officer of the constituency where the applicant ordinarily resides.The form requires basic details such as the applicant's name, details of a relative, Aadhaar information, gender, date of birth and present ordinary residence. Applicants are also required to complete a declaration, with the guidelines warning that making a false statement in it is punishable under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.The Election Commission's instructions also mandates that an applicant can fill the form either in English or in the official language of the state. Also, an applicant who does not know the number or name of the relevant constituency cannot have the application rejected merely for that reason.For age verification, applicants can submit a self-attested copy of one of the documents specified in the form. The guidelines also provide for verification by the Electoral Registration Officer in cases where the prescribed documents are unavailable.The Form 6Form_6_EnglishThe dispute over Form 6The petitions allege that additional requirements connected with the SIR were introduced into Form 6 through the Election Commission's software.One of the allegations is that details concerning an applicant's ancestry (details of father or grandfather) and a link to the previous SIR were incorporated into the process without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.The petitioners have further alleged that Election Commissioner Vivek Joshi objected to the modification and that Election Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu subsequently endorsed the objection. Therefore, the issue therefore goes beyond the information sought from voters.At the heart of the dispute is whether the Election Commission could alter the form and introduce SIR-linked requirements through its software without following the legal process required for changing the relevant electoral rules. During the hearing, the CJI specifically flagged the question of who authorised the modification.“Any modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When record has produced, we would like to see who has modified. But, your prayers appear jumbled up,” the CJI noted, as quoted by LiveLaw.The court, however, did not accept the petitioners' allegations as established facts at this stage as Justice Bagchi said the court would first need responses from the concerned authorities and records before deciding whether any decision was taken contrary to the statutory framework.Also Read | 'Form 6 has not been approved by us': What SC said on EC's SIR decision - top quotes"If records show some decision was not unanimous etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra-vires. Can we ex-parte come to decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner," Justice Bagchi added.EC retracts on From 6Amid the raging controvery, the Election Commission withdrew the additional SIR-related declaration from Form 6 in states where the electoral roll revision exercise had been completed.In states where the SIR was concluded, the EC removed additional declaration from the ECINET app and portal, as well as the respective Chief Electoral Officer portals. This meant that applicants in states where SIR is over will only need to fill the regular statutory Form 6 to enrol as voters.Just days before this action and as the controvery over dissent in the poll body emerged, the EC in a press note had, however, said that "the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used."The larger SIR controversyThe Form 6 dispute forms part of a broader challenge to how the Election Commission has allegedly handled the SIR exercise. The petitions rely on claims that the two other Election Commissioners formally raised objections on at least 14 occasions over several months to decisions and orders concerning the revision of electoral rolls.The allegations include changes to electoral-roll software, communications issued in the name of the Election Commission and other decisions allegedly taken without the approval of all members of the multi-member poll panel.The petitioners have invoked Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023. The provision states that the Commission's business should, as far as possible, be transacted unanimously and that where the members differ, the matter is to be decided according to the majority view.The pleas argue that this framework means powers vested in the Election Commission cannot be exercised individually by the CEC where the law requires the Commission to act collectively.The petitioners have sought several forms of relief, including suspension of Gyanesh Kumar as CEC until the matter is decided, preservation of electoral-roll data and audit trails, and restrictions on further substantive changes to Form 6.Another plea has sought criminal proceedings against the CEC and other officials and argued that decisions, guidelines and software changes allegedly made without the full Commission's agreement should be declared unconstitutional, ultra vires and void ab initio.The Supreme Court has therefore, at this stage, not ruled on whether the alleged changes to Form 6 or other SIR-related decisions were unlawful. The immediate question before the court is whether the Election Commission followed the statutory decision-making process.The court will consider the records and responses of the respondents before deciding whether any particular decision can be struck down.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1990, Wisconsin used up to 20,000 tons of foundry sand in a highway project; by 2002, a contract called for 80,000 tons for Highway 10
articles.summary: A research project in Wisconsin in the mid-1980s eventually led to the planned reuse of tens of thousands of tons of spent foundry sand in highway
articles.body: A research project in Wisconsin in the mid-1980s eventually led to the planned reuse of tens of thousands of tons of spent foundry sand in highway construction. Waupaca Foundry participated in a University of Wisconsin-Madison research study examining whether used foundry sand could be reused in road projects. Sand from Waupaca and two other foundries was tested for potential environmental impacts, including contaminants in pore water and leachate. In 1990, the research was followed by a pilot project with the Wisconsin Department of Transportation, in which between 15,000 and 20,000 tons of Waupaca's sand were used in highway construction. By the time of an EPA case study published in October 2002, Waupaca was under contract to provide 80,000 tons of sand as structural fill for embankments on Highway 10 near the city of Waupaca.How Waupaca Foundry's used sand was prepared for Highway 10The larger Highway 10 project required the material to be moved and stored before construction. For 10 months starting in 2001, Waupaca hauled its foundry sand to a temporary staging area near the future highway site, ahead of construction work planned for summer 2002. Because of the foundry's production process, the sand could be used directly as fill without additional screening or treatment. The embankment was to be closely monitored with lysimeters to check for leaching. The monitoring plan required Waupaca to investigate the cause of any exceedance, test the collected leachate and propose a response if Wisconsin's limits were exceeded. The Wisconsin Department of Transportation also planned to place a clay cap over the completed fill. The EPA case study describes this monitoring as planned and does not report monitoring results for the Highway 10 embankment.Wisconsin's rules classified foundry sand according to its propertiesThe reuse of foundry sand was governed by Wisconsin Administrative Code Chapter NR 538, the state's framework for the beneficial use of industrial by-products. Under the system described in the EPA case study, materials were placed into categories according to their characteristics, with Category 1 materials facing the fewest restrictions. Materials seeking Category 1 or Category 2 status had to meet standards for their overall composition as well as leachate quality and quantity. Waupaca's sand met Category 1 requirements for all tested constituents except arsenic and barium, which were at Category 2 levels. Before its agreement with the DOT, Waupaca had to obtain an initial certification covering its waste collection process and the composition and physical properties of its sand. To maintain its certification for highway embankment use, the company was required to submit annual information on production and use, along with evidence that the material continued to meet its classification and summaries of environmental monitoring. The EPA case study also notes that certain large projects, such as those involving more than 100,000 cubic yards of industrial by-products, require concurrence from the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources.The sand was described as comparable to conventional fillThe EPA case study states that foundry sand performs on par with fresh borrow or fill material when used as structural fill in highway construction. It also states that in areas with clay-rich soils, foundry sand can be superior to conventional borrow. The Waupaca sand was described as uniform and similar to virgin sand, although it was finer, smoother and black in colour. The black colour limited some potential applications. The case study attributes to the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources the view that the sand's dark colour limits its potential use, noting that aesthetic considerations prevent black sand from being used without cover or encapsulation. The report also says that the Wisconsin DOT had reported no problems with foundry sand use and that lysimeter levels had remained within DNR specifications. These statements concern the foundry-sand projects discussed in the case study generally; the report does not provide monitoring results for the Highway 10 embankment.Reuse costs were close to other fill and disposal optionsFor the Highway 10 project, the estimated total cost of using Waupaca's foundry sand was approximately $9 to $9.25 per ton, including transportation, monitoring and maintenance. The EPA case study said the cost was comparable to disposing of the material in Waupaca's company-owned off-site monofill, although reuse was somewhat more expensive than the initial cost of monofilling. Waupaca also estimated that reuse was similar in cost to using a commercial or municipal landfill. Wisconsin DOT staff said the overall cost was comparable to using virgin fill, as the lower cost of the reused material was offset by the additional cost of the lining. It explains that the lower cost of the reused material was offset by the additional cost of the lining. Transportation was another important factor because the economics of reuse depended on how far the material had to be moved. The case study described about 40 miles as the maximum feasible transport distance for the project when a local staging area was available.The EPA's October 2002 case study documented the progression from a 15,000-to-20,000-ton highway pilot project in 1990 to a contract for 80,000 tons of structural fill for Highway 10. It described the project within Wisconsin's system for testing, classifying and monitoring industrial by-products for beneficial reuse, while also identifying transportation and lining costs as important considerations. The case study describes monitoring of the Highway 10 embankment as planned and does not report subsequent monitoring or performance results for that project.You use AI every day. articles.title: Watch: Russian soldier takes down Ukrainian drone with portable air defence system near Moscow
articles.summary: A video of a Russian soldier firing a man-portable air defence system at a Ukrainian drone flying at low altitude over a major highway in the Moscow
articles.body: A video of a Russian soldier firing a man-portable air defence system at a Ukrainian drone flying at low altitude over a major highway in the Moscow region, with footage of the reported engagement has emerged amid intensified drone attacks between Russia and Ukraine.The footage, shared on X by social media news aggregator Visegrád 24, allegedly shows a Russian soldier operating a 9K38 Igla man-portable air-defence system. The Soviet-era Igla, also known as a man-portable air-defence system (MANPADS), is designed to engage low-flying aircraft and drones. It uses an infrared seeker to detect heat signatures, particularly from aircraft engines, and guide the missile towards its target.According to specifications cited by the CIA, the Igla entered service in 1983 and uses a solid-fuel rocket motor. It weighs about 10.8kg and has an operational range of around 5.2km, with a flight ceiling of approximately 3.5km. Its peak speed is about 800 metres per second.The reported engagement comes as Ukraine has stepped up its use of long-range drones against targets inside Russia, including areas far from the front line. Moscow and surrounding regions have repeatedly reported drone attacks, with Russian authorities saying air-defence units have intercepted large numbers of unmanned aerial vehicles.On Sunday, Russia’s defence ministry claimed that its forces carried out strikes against Ukrainian military-linked targets, including areas around Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and cargo vessels in the Odesa region.Recently, in overnight assault, Russian authorities reported that more than 1,900 Ukrainian drones, along with eight guided bombs, eight cruise missiles and four rockets, had been shot down. Earlier, Russian officials reported casualties and damage from another drone attack, including three deaths and damage to an oil refinery. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said one attack “was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections”.Additionally, Ukraine said on Sunday that its long-range strikes had put 51 per cent of Russia’s oil-refining capacity out of action, potentially affecting Moscow’s ability to supply its forces. Ukraine’s defence ministry said recent strikes targeted refineries in Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran.Both sides have intensified aerial attacks as fighting along the 1,200-kilometre front line has largely stalled. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries earlier this year also contributed to fuel shortages and restrictions on petrol sales.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2015, a Kansas neighbour building a boundary fence cut 133 trees, some as far as 70 feet inside the adjoining land; 11 years later, an appeals court has upheld the landowner’s $6,500 damages award
articles.summary: A Kansas appeals court on Friday, upheld a $6,500 damages award against a man whose fence-building project led to 133 trees being cut on a neighbour’s
articles.body: A Kansas appeals court on Friday, upheld a $6,500 damages award against a man whose fence-building project led to 133 trees being cut on a neighbour’s property in 2015. According to legal research website Justia, the court rejected several challenges raised by accused Douglas H Black, including arguments that the lawsuit was filed too late and that the damages were not properly calculated.The complainant was Jason Deal, who owns about 120 acres of recreational property in Woodson County, Kansas. In March 2015, a fence was rebuilt along the boundary between Deal’s property and land owned at the time by his neighbour, Ivan Black. The fence ran for about 300 feet along the top of a bluff.Douglas Black, Ivan’s son, helped build the fence with his brother Mitch Black, William “Ricky” Ward and Yancy Wade, who was Douglas’ stepson. Ivan bought the materials and paid Ward and Wade for the work. However, no survey was carried out before construction to confirm exactly where the property boundary lay.During the work, Wade cut trees in the area where the new fence was being built. He also cut trees that hung over the planned fence and trees that were considered likely to fall on it. The trees were also left where they fell.The location later became central to the legal dispute because it was difficult to reach from Deal’s side of the property. He could only access it on foot, crossing a creek and climbing a rock bluff. Deal usually visited that part of his land only once a year, mainly in spring to look for shed antlers.Deal discovered trees a year laterDeal said he discovered the fallen trees and the new fence in March 2016, about a year after the fence work. He contacted Ivan Black, but said he received little information. He then contacted Douglas, who confirmed that he had been responsible for cutting the trees.Deal found that trees had been cut as far as 70 feet from the old fence line. In total, 133 trees on his property had been felled.Deal then filed a lawsuit against Douglas in December 2017, alleging trespass and seeking damages for the destroyed trees. Douglas challenged the case on several grounds, including the argument that Deal had waited too long to sue.The case did not reach trial quickly. There were several delays and continuances, including some connected to the Covid-19 pandemic, settlement discussions and problems involving the lawyers. A bench trial was eventually held in October 2024.Deal told the court that the property had personal and biological importance to him. He has a degree in Fisheries and Wildlife biology and had worked as a public lands regional supervisor. He said he bought the property because it formed part of the Cross Timbers ecosystem and described work he had carried out to improve wildlife habitat, including removing invasive species.Valuation of the treesBoth sides brought experts to court to discuss the value of the damaged trees. Deal hired consulting forester Ryan Neises. Neises examined the trees that had been cut and identified 115 post oaks, five hickories, five red oaks, two red cedars, two green ashes, two American elms, one hackberry and one redbud. Using his calculations, Neises valued the damage at $13,799.96. Deal also hired forest ecologist and conservation consultant Kevin Church. Using Neises' observations but a different method of calculation, Church placed the value of the downed trees at $61,497.61.Meanwhile, Douglas hired consulting arborist and tree expert Ivan Katzer. He estimated the damages at about $1,273. Katzer said there was no loss of income, no demonstrable effect on the market value of the land and no timber or amenity value for the particular trees.The district court did not accept either of the experts' figures as the final amount. In August 2025, it ruled that Wade had trespassed onto Deal’s property when trees were cut well beyond the fence line. Because Wade was found to be Douglas' agent, the court held Douglas responsible for the damage.The court awarded Deal $6,500. It also reduced that amount by $400 to account for attorney fees Douglas had incurred because of a last-minute trial continuance requested by Deal’s lawyer.Appeals court says lawsuit filed on timeDouglas challenged the ruling before the Kansas Court of Appeals. One of his main arguments was that Deal's trespass claim should have been dismissed under the state's two-year statute of limitations. The appeals court disagreed.Kansas law provides a two-year period for bringing a trespass action. However, the period can begin when the injury becomes reasonably ascertainable if the damage was not reasonably discoverable when the act occurred.The court noted that the tree cutting took place in March 2015. However, it also accepted the district court's finding that the affected part of Deal’s property was extremely difficult to reach from his side. Douglas himself acknowledged during testimony that reaching the area from Deal's property was “Extremely difficult.”The appeals court found there was enough evidence to support the district court's conclusion that Deal could not reasonably have discovered the damage immediately. Deal discovered the trees in March 2016 and filed his lawsuit in December 2017.Court upholds damages and trespass findingThe appeals court also rejected Douglas' argument that the $6,500 award was unsupported. The district court had considered the value of the trees, the value of the land and the trees' intrinsic value. It also considered the fact that the damaged area covered about half an acre of Deal's 118-acre tract and that he visited that remote section only once a year.The appeals court said there was no clear and universal rule for measuring damages when trees are destroyed. It found that the district court had properly balanced the different factors before reaching its award.The court also upheld the finding that Douglas had trespassed. While Kansas law allows an adjoining landowner to enter neighbouring property at reasonable times and in a reasonable manner to repair or rebuild a partition fence, the appeals court said that did not justify clearing a 30-foot strip of Deal's land.The district court had found that trees within the fence line were not part of Deal's claim. The damages instead related to trees cut farther onto his property.Finally, the appeals court upheld Douglas' responsibility for the full damages. Although Wade physically cut the trees, Douglas had testified that he was in charge of the crew and had instructed Wade to cut trees that could fall on the fence.The court found sufficient evidence of an agency relationship between Douglas and Wade. It therefore found no error in holding Douglas fully responsible for the damages.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Thailand floods wreak havoc as death toll rises to 31, more rain forecast - video
articles.summary: Thailand warned of more heavy rain and flash flooding on Monday as the death toll from floods across the country since September 16 rose to 31,
articles.body: Thailand warned of more heavy rain and flash flooding on Monday as the death toll from floods across the country since September 16 rose to 31, authorities said. More than 3.5 million people remained affected nationwide, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation.Heavy rain flooded Bangkok over the weekend and into Monday, leaving roads and neighbourhoods waterlogged. Videos showed people wading through knee-deep water, cars submerged and supermarkets and shops operating despite floodwaters covering their floors.Many areas were inundated last week after days of torrential rain. The city's conditions have largely improved, although floodwaters remain in some lower-lying areas.In one video, residents could be seen continuing their daily routines inside flooded shops, while another showed vehicles almost totally submerged in water. Locals also turned a flooded street outside a shopping mall into a temporary floating market, with sellers wading through the water and using floating platforms and foam boxes to sell fish and vegetables.Bangkok was declared a disaster-affected zone after continuous heavy rain caused widespread flooding. Schools remained closed for a second day in several areas, while many residents worked from home. Flooding also caused travel disruptions at Bangkok’s airports, major regional hubs.Thailand’s Meteorological Department warned that thunderstorms, strong winds and heavy rain were expected across much of upper Thailand from Monday through Wednesday, increasing the risk of flash floods, particularly in low-lying areas.Very heavy to heavy rain was also forecast in parts of the central, eastern and southern regions, including Bangkok. City authorities said they were draining more water from major canals to increase their capacity and deploying additional pumps in high-risk areas.The flooding has affected eight provinces, with four of the reported deaths in Bangkok. The government last week approved emergency funds of more than 4.1 billion baht, about $122 million, for flood recovery.The flooding has also disrupted Thailand’s aviation sector. Thai Airways dismissed its chief executive, Chai Eamsiril, on Friday following flight delays and baggage backlogs linked to the Bangkok flooding, local media reported.Eamsiril had apologised on behalf of the airline and pledged to clear more than 5,000 bags stranded at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi airport. articles.title: Psychology says children who create secret hiding places at home may be doing more than just playing
articles.summary: A blanket over two chairs. A space behind the sofa. A corner under the dining table.
articles.body: A blanket over two chairs. A space behind the sofa. A corner under the dining table. A cardboard box turned into a “house” that nobody else is allowed to enter. For some children, an ordinary corner of the house can quickly become a secret place. They may tell parents, “You can't come in,” give the place a name, take toys inside or simply sit there alone for a while. To adults, it can look like another game. But research on children's secret hiding places suggests these spaces can also give children a sense of ownership, privacy, safety and control over a small part of their environment.Why do children create secret hiding places?Children do not always need a large or elaborate space. A blanket, bedsheet, cardboard box or an unused corner can be enough. A 2016 study looked at how preschool children created their own spaces. The researchers found that children preferred flexible materials such as blankets, bedsheets and cardboard tubes and often worked together to build their spaces. The resulting spaces could provide a form of refuge for children. This suggests that a hiding place can be more than somewhere to play. It can become a small area that feels like it belongs to the child.“This is my place”Ownership is an important part of the behaviour. In an earlier study of 100 children aged three to five in daycare settings, 58 said they had a special place that they considered their own. These included spaces such as a cubby, a chair or a hiding place under a playhouse. Some children also identified a special place at home. Children may not have much control over where they live, when they eat, when they sleep or what adults ask them to do. A small space that they can arrange themselves gives them at least some control over their surroundings. That does not mean every child who hides under a table is asking for more independence. But creating a space of their own can give children an opportunity to decide who enters, what happens there and what the space means to them.The hiding place can become emotionally importantA particularly interesting study looked directly at 17 preschool children aged three to five and their experiences with secret hiding places. In the results, children described spaces that were sometimes kept off limits to other people. Researchers found that these places could have individual, relational and collaborative purposes. Children also connected secret spaces with excitement, imagination and intimacy. In other words, “secret” did not necessarily mean something bad was happening.Privacy can be part of growing independenceAs children grow, wanting some control over what they share and who has access to their personal space becomes increasingly important. Research on children's privacy suggests that children actively create territories within shared environments rather than simply accepting the spaces adults provide for them. A special corner can therefore become one of the early ways children experience having a boundary of their own. This is different from encouraging children to keep harmful secrets. A child having a secret playhouse under a table is very different from a child being told to hide something that makes them uncomfortable or afraid. Parents can respect a child's private play space while still making it clear that unsafe secrets should always be shared with a trusted adult.What happens inside the secret space mattersThe space itself may tell parents very little. What the child does there can be more informative. Some children may take books, dolls or stuffed toys inside and create elaborate games. Others may use the space to draw, read or simply lie down. Some may invite one particular friend or sibling but not adults. A 2023 research on children's secret hiding places found that children can develop emotional connections with these spaces through the activities they carry out there. The researchers noted that children sometimes described hiding places as special or favourite places and that some children associated them with comfort when they were sad or upset.Should parents leave children alone?Usually, there is no need to immediately dismantle a harmless hiding place simply because the child wants adults to stay out. Parents can say, “Okay, this is your space. I'll knock before I come in.” That gives the child a boundary while keeping the parent connected. It is also useful to ask simple questions rather than interrogate the child: “What do you like doing in here?” or “What makes this place special?” If the child wants to show the space, let them. If they want a little privacy during play, that can also be respected. At the same time, parents should pay attention if hiding becomes a sudden and extreme change accompanied by persistent sadness, fear, withdrawal, avoidance of family members, school refusal or signs that the child is trying to escape a situation that feels unsafe.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Fighting this battle in our own way': AAP to skip opposition march to EC office over SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on Monday said it would not participate in the Congress-led opposition INDIA bloc's march to the Election Commission
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on Monday said it would not participate in the Congress-led opposition INDIA bloc's march to the Election Commission office, saying it was "fighting this battle in our own way."Senior AAP leader and Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Singh said protests against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were being held daily at different places across the country.He added that the AAP was not even using its own banner, as it considers the issue a "people's movement" concerning citizens across the country and believes everyone should participate in it."The CJP's (Cockroach Janta Party) protest is also being held, and different organisations are also holding protests. The Left is also protesting in different places. As far as tomorrow's protest is concerned, it is the INDIA bloc's protest. So, the AAP is not part of it. We are fighting this battle in our own way," Singh told reporters at the Parliament House complex.Two parties formerly aligned with the INDIA bloc, the AAP and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), had also skipped the alliance's September 30 meeting to decide its response to an Indian Express report concerning the EC. Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav was absent as well, but sent party representatives to attend the meeting.Some other leaders, including Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray and Jharkhand chief minister and Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM) president Hemant Soren, participated virtually.After the meeting, attended by the Congress and 18 other opposition parties, INDIA bloc leaders announced that they and all its MPs would march to the Election Commission's headquarters in the capital on October 6. The leaders would also meet President Droupadi Murmu to raise concerns over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls.The call for the protest came amid a controversy over the functioning of the EC, with opposition parties alleging irregularities in the poll panel's handling of the SIR exercise.An investigation by The Indian Express last month reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected on record at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, which they alleged had been issued without their knowledge or recommendation. Sandhu and Joshi also reportedly termed specific changes made to voter enrolment forms "unauthorised" and "illegal".The EC has rejected suggestions of a split within the three-member panel, maintaining that decisions relating to the SIR were taken unanimously.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A 250-pound WWII bomb was found underwater near Falmouth Docks; more than 300 homes were evacuated before it could be removed
articles.summary: Hundreds of homes in Falmouth, Cornwall, were evacuated in September after a suspected 250-pound American bomb from the Second World War was found in the
articles.body: Hundreds of homes in Falmouth, Cornwall, were evacuated in September after a suspected 250-pound American bomb from the Second World War was found in the water near Falmouth Docks. A diver discovered the unexploded device on 21st September, and the exclusion zone was widened two days later. More than 300 homes were cleared by 23rd September, and residents returned that afternoon after the bomb was safely removed from the docks. Final disposal in deep water well out at sea was planned for several days later, once divers could return.When a diver found a suspected 250-pound American Second World War bomb in the sea at Falmouth DocksThe BBC reported that emergency services were called to Falmouth Docks at a quarter past nine in the morning on Monday 21st September. A suspected air-dropped bomb of about 250 pounds, or 115 kilograms, had been found in the water. Tom Bolt of Falmouth Coastguard told the BBC that a diver came across the device and alerted the coastguard. The Ministry of Defence was called in, and experts assessed the situation and confirmed what it was.South West News Service reporter Filipa Gaspar wrote that police clarified the unexploded device found in the water near the docks was believed to be a 250-pound, or 113-kilogram, American air-dropped bomb from the Second World War. She added that authorities had earlier reported its weight as 250 kilograms rather than pounds.Why more than 300 homes and about 2,000 people were cleared as officials expanded the exclusion zoneThe BBC said a 300-metre exclusion zone was put in place on Tuesday and expanded to 755 metres on Wednesday. Residents of more than 300 homes were asked to leave before nine o’clock in the morning, ahead of the bomb being moved. The broadcaster said the evacuation involved about 2,000 people.South West News Service reported that the zone took effect at nine o’clock on Wednesday morning and covered multiple postcodes. It said the estimate of 339 homes was about 1,000 fewer than the 1,300 first estimated, when the cordon was set at 1.4 kilometres. The cordon had been reduced at seven o’clock the previous evening. Emergency services, council staff and volunteers knocked on doors to help residents leave. Superintendent Ian Thompson, policing commander for West Cornwall, put the figure at some 336 households. Both outlets reported that the operation involved 81 police officers and staff, along with 113 volunteers and colleagues from partner agencies.Why a 144-hour delay chemical fuse forced Royal Navy divers to leave this unusual bomb on the seabedLieutenant Commander Ben Brown, commanding officer of the Bravo Diving Squadron, told the BBC that the bomb was an American device with a 144-hour delay chemical fuse. He said contact with the device could have set that fuse off. It lay on the seabed in about 20 metres of water, with a 500-metre exclusion zone around it. Brown said: “This device is unusual, and we must now wait for a further six days.” After the wait, divers would attach a small charge to complete the disposal.South West News Service reported that the bomb was first moved to a safer location within the docks before being removed for disposal. Cornwall Council confirmed before four o’clock in the afternoon on Wednesday that the device had been safely removed from Falmouth Docks. The cordon was lifted, and residents were allowed home. The council said the bomb would be disposed of in deep water well out at sea, with nothing to see or hear from the shore. The reports reviewed for this article did not confirm that the final disposal had been completed.What police, councillors, and residents said as All Saints’ Church became a help centre for evacueesThe BBC reported that All Saints’ Church in Falmouth served as a help centre, where displaced residents were given tea, coffee and somewhere to sit. Folk singer Will Keating, one of those asked to leave home, sang and played guitar to lift spirits. Jean Elsie, aged 92, said she had lived through the war in south London and did not mind much. Maureen Gill, aged 89, had assumed the closed road was for roadworks until she heard the news on the radio.Thalia Marrington, the Cornwall councillor responsible for public safety, called the removal of the device “the news everyone wanted to hear”, according to South West News Service. She thanked military specialists, emergency services, council teams and volunteers, as well as residents and businesses for their patience during a worrying and disruptive time. Superintendent Thompson confirmed that all cordons had been lifted and that the multi-agency operation had concluded. He thanked the Falmouth community for its patience and praised the skill and bravery of the military bomb disposal experts.How a historian explained the plausible reasons an American air-dropped bomb ended up in the harbourIt is not known for certain why the bomb ended up there. Catriona Pennell, a professor of modern history and memory studies at the University of Exeter, told the BBC that an American aircraft might have jettisoned it, either because of a technical fault or an abandoned mission. Another possibility is that it rolled off a ship unloading at the docks. She noted that large aircraft such as the Liberator were designed to hunt German submarines in the Atlantic, and that a bomb like this was built to destroy them.You use AI every day.
